findings.headline: Your NSF fee is the highest in your peer set.
findings.body: At $32.00, your NSF fee tops every one of the five comparable large credit unions with published data — more than double the $15 median, and flagged as an extreme outlier. One peer in the set has eliminated the fee entirely. The contrast is sharpened by the rest of your schedule, which is otherwise notably member-friendly: this is the one line that tells a different story.

findings.headline: You waive fees your peers still charge.
findings.body: Non-network ATM transactions ($0 against a $1.00 peer median) and minimum-balance charges ($0 against a $4.00 median) are waived outright on your schedule. These are exactly the small, frequent frictions members notice — and exactly the claims that comparison-minded members verify against published schedules. Today neither waiver appears anywhere in your marketing.

findings.headline: Your service-fee stack runs well below market.
findings.body: Card replacement ($5.00 vs a $25.00 median, 31st percentile), overdraft-protection transfers ($5.00 vs a $20.00 median), and stop payments ($10.00 vs $15.00, 33rd percentile) all price under most comparable credit unions. Combined with the waived fees above, this is a coherent member-value posture — undermined only by the NSF outlier, and unclaimed as a story.

exec_narrative: Net position: Dfcu Financial runs one of the more member-friendly published schedules in its cohort — two fees waived outright, a service-fee stack below market — with a single glaring exception: a $32 NSF fee that is the highest among the five comparable large credit unions with published data and more than double their median. One caveat on the data: peer samples in this cohort are thin (four to thirteen institutions for most categories), so percentiles should be read as directional. The strategic question is coherence: either the NSF fee comes into line with the rest of the schedule, or the member-value story stays untellable because its biggest counterexample sits on page one of the fee schedule.

callouts.title: NSF / returned item — $32.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $15.00 · P25 $7.00 · 100th percentile · n=5 · flagged: extreme outlier (>2x median)
callouts.body: The peer set is small, but its shape is unambiguous: the median is $15, a quarter of the set charges $7 or less, and one comparable credit union has retired the fee altogether. At $32 you hold the top of the distribution during an industry-wide retreat from NSF fees. For an institution whose other fees signal member value, this line is the outlier in both senses — statistical and strategic. It warrants a decision: cut, cap, or a documented rationale.

callouts.title: Waived fees — $0 where peers charge
callouts.stat: ATM non-network $0.00 vs $1.00 median · Minimum balance $0.00 vs $4.00 median
callouts.body: Two fees your peers still charge, you have eliminated. These waivers are verifiable in your published schedule and directly comparable against peers' — which makes them low-risk marketing claims with real substance. A member choosing between large credit unions can confirm the difference in five minutes; today, nothing invites them to look.

callouts.title: Service fees — priced below market, marketed nowhere
callouts.stat: Card replacement $5.00 vs $25.00 median (P31) · OD protection transfer $5.00 vs $20.00 median · Stop payment $10.00 vs $15.00 median (P33)
callouts.body: Three consumer-facing service fees run at a fraction of the cohort median. If deliberate, they complete a member-value narrative that spans the whole schedule and deserves to be told. If not deliberate, they are margin available without touching a headline fee. The one move to avoid is the current default: below market, and invisible.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the retreat from NSF: the largest institutions have largely eliminated returned-item fees, and the pressure has migrated across the industry — visible even in your small peer set, where the median has fallen to $15 and one comparable credit union charges nothing. Second, published fee schedules have become marketing documents: public, scraped, and compared, which converts every outlier line into a reputational bet and every waiver into a verifiable claim.

Large community credit unions occupy the exposed middle of that landscape: big enough to appear in every comparison and press survey, without the brand gravity that lets money-center banks price premiums quietly. What credit unions at your scale do have is the member-ownership story — and your schedule already substantiates it almost everywhere. In that position the highest-leverage move is rarely an across-the-board cut; it is resolving the single conspicuous outlier so the rest of the schedule can be advertised without an asterisk.
